source.title_on_document: Dialogue patterns in human-AI co-creation: how interaction structure shapes output and process

supplement.where: No separate supplementary material or online appendix is identified in the document. Appendices A (system prompts), B (dialogue-act coding scheme), and C (coding validation, Table C1) are inside this PDF, PDF pp. 30-32 (journal pp. 29-31). Section 5.8, titled 'Supplementary analyses', is part of the main text (PDF pp. 23-24). The data availability statement says the datasets are not publicly available but can be requested from the corresponding author (PDF p. 27, journal p. 26).
supplement.holds: No statistics are identified as available only in an external supplement. In the supplied PDF, per-arm originality means for all arms and appropriateness means for HLE and FD appear only as bars in Figure 4 (PDF p. 16); descriptive-richness standard errors appear only as error bars in Figure 5 (PDF p. 21). Numerical standard errors for the rated outcomes and numerical bootstrap intervals for Figure 7 are not printed.

paper_design_summary: US Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were randomly assigned with sequential balancing to four Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite interaction designs: human-lead expand (HLE), AI-lead propose (ALP), iterative critique (IC), and free dialogue (FD); 244 people were analyzed after exclusions (PDF pp. 9-11, Sections 4.1-4.4 and Table 1). Each wrote a user persona and usage scenario for a gardening seed-trading app, which three blinded external judges rated for originality and appropriateness, summed into a creativity score out of 20 (PDF pp. 10-13, Sections 4.2-4.5.1). All arms used AI, and the paper also computes descriptive richness and between-persona embedding similarity within each condition (PDF p. 14, Sections 4.5.4-4.5.5).

studies.label: Online between-subjects experiment with four AI interaction designs (persona and scenario writing)

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of four AI interaction designs: human-lead expand (HLE), AI-lead propose (ALP), iterative critique (IC), free dialogue (FD). Every arm used the same LLM with condition-specific interfaces and system prompts; there is no no-AI arm.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition and completed a user persona creation task with AI assistance structured according to their assigned pattern.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 8), Section 4.1; same page: 'Random assignment employed sequential balancing to ensure approximately equal group sizes across conditions.'; analyzed arm sizes in Figure 2 and Table 1, PDF p. 10
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 8), Section 4.2: 'Substantial exclusions were applied based on pre-registered quality criteria'. Only the exclusion criteria are described as pre-registered; no registry, link, preregistered hypothesis, or preregistered outcome is given.

arms.name: HLE (human-lead expand)
arms.description: Participant writes in the workspace and picks AI actions from a dropdown menu (generate demographic details, suggest scenario ideas, expand on goals, identify frustrations or challenges, elaborate personality traits); the AI generates content from the current draft and shows it in a separate panel that the participant integrates by hand.

arms.name: ALP (AI-lead propose)
arms.description: The AI first shows five persona concepts as cards (Section 4.4.2 names a persona name and demographic sketch); the participant selects one and develops it in the editor. The AI stays available in chat, can see but not change the workspace, and its system prompt limits it to elaborating the chosen proposal. The initial-generation prompt also requests a motivation, frustration, and scenario suggestion; the paper does not specify whether all these details appeared on the cards (PDF pp. 11-12, Section 4.4.2; PDF p. 30, Appendix A).

arms.name: IC (iterative critique)
arms.description: Participant drafts alone and clicks 'Get Feedback' as often as wished; the AI returns structured critique (strengths, areas for improvement, recommendations, 2-3 points each) and produces no drafts.

arms.name: FD (free dialogue)
arms.description: Split-pane free chat with the AI beside the participant's workspace; the AI can view but not edit the workspace. Its system prompt includes an evaluation-rubric summary and asks it to be constructively critical and guide the user toward those criteria (PDF p. 12, Section 4.4.4; PDF p. 31, Appendix A).

participants.exclusions: Section 4.2 reports 275 initially assigned 'participants' and 31 exclusions, leaving 244 analyzed people. The initial count is not confirmed as distinct people: one exclusion rule removes repeat completions identified by MTurk worker ID or coordinated submissions from the same IP address, retaining only the first valid submission. The other stated pre-registered quality rules exclude fewer than 3 logged interactions or completion in under 3 minutes, and submissions flagged by research assistants for bot-like behavior, nonsensical content, or clear inattention. The 31 exclusions are not broken down by rule or arm, so the number of distinct people randomized and each arm's randomized count are null. Analyzed arm counts are HLE 60, ALP 62, IC 61, and FD 61 (PDF p. 10, Table 1 and Figure 2). The analysis uses the 244 retained, so it is not intention-to-treat. Figure 2 places the final sample before random assignment, whereas Section 4.2 describes exclusions after assignment; the text's chronology is retained with this source conflict flagged.
participants.who: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers in the United States with a HIT approval rate of 99 percent or higher and at least 1000 prior HITs; $2 base pay plus $10-$30 bonuses for top-rated submissions. Mean age 38.1; 54 percent male (Table 1).
participants.quote: A total of 275 participants were initially assigned to one of four human–AI interaction patterns. After applying the predefined data quality criteria, 31 participants were excluded, resulting in a final sample of 244 participants.
participants.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 8), Section 4.2; arm counts in Figure 2 and Table 1, PDF p. 10 (journal p. 9)

ai_tool.name_model: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (preview release 09/2025), accessed through OpenRouter as google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite-preview-09-2025, with condition-specific system prompts (Appendix A, PDF pp. 30-31)
ai_tool.how_used: Role differs by arm. HLE: menu-triggered AI content generated from the participant's draft and shown in a separate panel for manual integration (nearest code ideas_supplied, given on request; not inline, so not suggestions). ALP: the AI supplies five starting persona concepts (ideas_supplied), then chat limited to elaborating the chosen one. IC: structured critique of the participant's own draft on request, with no drafts written (refinement). FD: free chat beside the workspace (open_chat), with an evaluation-rubric summary and a constructively critical system prompt (Appendix A, PDF p. 31). In all arms only the participant could write in the workspace.

task.description: Create a user persona (name, demographics, description) and a usage scenario for a hypothetical mobile app that helps local gardeners trade seeds and produce. The task is a design activity producing a narrative text artifact, coded creative_writing (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 4.3; PDF p. 12, Section 4.5).
task.duration: Advertised as about 20-40 min; mean logged task duration 10:13 (min:sec), by arm HLE 9:13, ALP 9:08, IC 10:36, FD 11:59 (Table 1, PDF p. 10). Single session.

outcomes.name: Composite creativity score (originality + appropriateness, out of 20)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of originality and appropriateness ratings (each on a 10-point scale), each the mean of three independent blinded external judges with backgrounds relevant to evaluating narrative artifacts (e.g., creative writing) (PDF pp. 12-13, Sections 4.5 and 4.5.1). ICC(3,3) = .84, 95% CI [.80, .87] (PDF p. 15, Section 4.6). Convergent-validity check against Qwen3-32B ratings of the same rubric: overall creativity r_s = .71 (not reported by condition). Sample mean 16.53 (SD 3.56) (Table 1, PDF p. 10). Omnibus Brown-Forsythe F(3, 199.14) = 2.88, p = .0437, eta^2 = .035, 95% CI [.000, .081] (PDF p. 16, Section 5.1.1). Figure 7 composite d for all six pairs (positive = left-hand condition higher; * = survives Holm across 6 pairs): HLE vs ALP +0.20, HLE vs IC -0.36, HLE vs FD +0.17, ALP vs IC -0.50*, ALP vs FD -0.02, IC vs FD +0.45 (PDF p. 23).

outcomes.name: Between-persona semantic similarity within condition (persona, scenario, and combined text)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity for every pair of personas, computed separately for persona content, scenario content, and concatenated persona-plus-scenario text, with two embedding models (six model-by-content cells). The reported inferential statistic is each condition's mean across its output pairs, tested against a permutation null from 10,000 condition-label shuffles; its analysis unit is the condition's whole pool of outputs (set), and pairs are not independent observations in this test (PDF p. 14, Section 4.5.5; PDF p. 21, Section 5.5). The between-condition baseline in Figure 6 is a separate descriptive comparison; the paper does not identify its values as permutation-null means, and numerical null means are not reported (PDF p. 22, Figure 6 caption). A length-controlled robustness variant projects out the length-correlated embedding direction and gives the same direction with larger z; the uncontrolled values are the paper's primary inference. Higher z means greater similarity and lower diversity, so contrast directions are coded on diversity with the sign reversed.

Separate descriptive comparison, within-condition cosine similarity vs between-condition baseline: nomic 0.718 vs 0.695; jina 0.833 vs 0.813. diversity_detail.metric: Within-condition mean pairwise cosine similarity, compared with a permutation null and reported as z with Holm-corrected two-sided p; the paper also frames it as semantic distance (1 minus cosine similarity), following Anderson et al. (2024).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: nomic-embed-text-v1.5 and jina-embeddings-v2-base-en (both 8,192-token maximum; no persona truncated, maximum observed 2,235 tokens)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of outputs within each condition, separately for persona content, scenario content, and concatenated persona-plus-scenario text; each tested statistic averages the pair similarities over that condition's whole pool of outputs. The null comes from 10,000 shuffles of condition labels across the 244 personas (PDF p. 14, Section 4.5.5).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Condition-level mean tested against a permutation distribution from 10,000 shuffles of condition labels; two-sided p with Holm-Bonferroni correction across the four conditions. Pairs supply similarities to the mean; they are not treated as independent observations in the reported test (PDF p. 14, Section 4.5.5; PDF p. 21, Section 5.5).
diversity_detail.notes: No direct arm-versus-arm diversity contrast is reported; each condition is compared with its permutation null. z and p are printed only for the IC and ALP cells named in the text; HLE and FD are described as nonsignificant, with distributions shown in Figure 6. Within-condition and between-condition baseline cosine values are printed only for the two effects that survive in both models. The descriptive between-condition baselines are not identified as permutation-null means; numerical null means remain unreported. Pair counts are not printed and no derived n_units is entered. Figure 7 does not include similarity.

outcomes.name: Descriptive richness (share of adjectives and adverbs in the text)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DR = (n_adj + n_adv) / n_tokens, punctuation excluded (PDF p. 14, Section 4.5.4). A computed word-class share, not a creativity scoring model; the authors treat it as a proxy for elaboration rather than writing quality and note it was not validated against human judgments (PDF p. 26, Section 6.5). The current codebook has no supported measure code for adjective-plus-adverb density; measure is null, while the formula and elaboration construct are retained. It is neither lexical overlap nor type-token variety. Omnibus Kruskal-Wallis H(3) = 19.06, p = .0003. Means: FD 0.149, ALP 0.142, HLE 0.141, IC 0.128; SEs only as error bars in Figure 5; SDs not printed. Not correlated with rated creativity (r_s = -0.101, p = .114). Figure 7 descriptive-richness d for all six pairs: HLE vs ALP +0.06, HLE vs IC +0.50*, HLE vs FD -0.33, ALP vs IC +0.43, ALP vs FD -0.38, IC vs FD -0.85* (PDF p. 23). The printed HLE-versus-ALP d is positive although the reported means place HLE below ALP; both source values are retained pending clarification (PDF p. 20, Section 5.4; PDF p. 23, Figure 7).

contrasts.reported: Means IC 0.128 vs FD 0.149. Dunn's test (Holm): FD > IC, p < .001, r = .43. Figure 7 row 'IC vs FD' d = -0.85* (negative = FD higher; survives Holm). SEs only as error bars in Figure 5. Only test statistic printed is the omnibus Kruskal-Wallis H(3) = 19.06, p = .0003; no pairwise statistic.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Section 4.1 explicitly reports random assignment of individuals to four AI interaction designs with sequential balancing (PDF p. 9); all use Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite for participants' own persona-and-scenario work (PDF p. 11, Section 4.4). The randomization procedure needs further detail, but the source expressly identifies assignment as random. There are 244 people analyzed after the quality exclusions, including removal of repeat completions, with HLE 60, ALP 62, IC 61, and FD 61 (PDF pp. 9-10, Section 4.2 and Table 1), satisfying the threshold on analyzed people. The reported 275 initial assignments are not confirmed as distinct people, so n_randomized is null; this does not change the analyzed count. Three blinded external judges scored originality, appropriateness, and composite creativity on the submitted artifacts, and similarity was computed across those outputs (PDF pp. 12-14, Sections 4.5-4.5.5). AI was available during production in every arm: rated-output arm comparisons are ai_design, while the reported diversity tests compare each condition's output pool with a permutation null.

one_line_finding: Among 244 MTurk workers analyzed across four randomly assigned AI interaction designs (no no-AI arm), iterative critique scored higher than AI-lead propose on composite creativity (17.57 vs 15.92 of 20; difference 1.64, 95% CI [.096, 3.191], p = .033) and appropriateness (8.65 vs 7.60, p = .022), originality did not differ (F(3, 240) = 2.42, p = .084) (PDF p. 16), and iterative-critique personas were more alike than a permutation null (nomic z = +2.59, p_holm = .037) while AI-lead propose combined outputs were more diverse (nomic z = -2.54, p_holm = .047) (PDF p. 21).
open_questions: Reference arm for ai_design contrasts: no condition is a plain default, and FD has an evaluation-rubric summary and a critical prompt (PDF p. 31, Appendix A). FD is retained as a descriptive reference alongside the paper's IC-versus-ALP contrast; selecting the primary contrast for pooling is an Atlas review decision, not a missing fact about eligibility.

Assignment mechanism: Section 4.1 says random assignment 'employed sequential balancing' but does not specify the allocation algorithm (PDF p. 9). The paper's explicit random-assignment statement supports the current coding; authors' allocation protocol or code would settle whether the balancing used a random element, which bears on criterion 1.

Participant-flow chronology: Figure 2 places the final sample of 244 before random assignment, whereas Section 4.2 reports 275 initial assignments and 31 exclusions afterwards (PDF pp. 9-10). The in-task exclusion rules support the text's chronology; authors could reconcile the diagram. This does not change the reported randomization or 244 analyzed people.

Distinct people randomized: 275 is the reported initial assignment count, but repeat completions by worker ID or IP were among the exclusion rules and no exclusions-by-rule breakdown is given (PDF p. 9, Section 4.2). The number of unique people assigned is unconfirmed, so n_randomized is null; authors' deduplicated participant flow would settle it. Criterion 2 uses the confirmed 244 analyzed people.

Exclusions after assignment: the 31 exclusions partly depend on AI engagement (fewer than 3 logged interactions or under 3 minutes), and exclusions by arm are not reported (PDF p. 9, Section 4.2). Authors' flow counts by arm and reason would permit assessment of differential exclusion; this is an attrition issue, not a failure of the analyzed-person threshold.

Preregistration: only the exclusion criteria are called pre-registered (PDF p. 9, Section 4.2), and the kappa interpretive rule was 'set in advance' (PDF p. 22, Section 5.6). No registry, link, or preregistered outcome is identified. Authors could supply the dated registration; composite creativity remains paper_primary from Section 4.2. Preregistration is not an eligibility criterion.

Source statistical inconsistencies: the printed originality and composite F/df/p combinations on PDF p. 16 and the trust and control combinations on PDF p. 17 are inconsistent. Figure 7 also prints a positive HLE-versus-ALP descriptive-richness d while the Section 5.4 means order HLE below ALP (PDF pp. 20, 23). Printed values are retained; corrected analysis output from the authors would settle these reporting issues without affecting eligibility.

Descriptive richness: measure is now null because no current measure code covers adjective-plus-adverb density; the source-defined formula and elaboration construct remain (PDF p. 14, Section 4.5.4; codebook Section 6). Any expanded measure vocabulary or decision about pooling this secondary outcome belongs to Atlas review. Other output-rated outcomes independently satisfy criterion 3.

Similarity: each condition's mean pairwise similarity is tested against a label-permutation null, with no direct arm-versus-arm diversity contrast printed (PDF pp. 14, 21-22). Numerical permutation-null means are not printed and cannot be replaced by the separate descriptive between-condition baseline. Authors' data and analysis output would settle the missing contrasts and null summaries; output-rated creativity already establishes criterion 3.

Task type: creative_writing is retained because the persona and scenario are narrative text artifacts (PDF pp. 10-12, Sections 4.3-4.5). Alternative task labels are a taxonomy decision; no further source is needed to establish that this is a creative task.

Unprinted outcome statistics: some originality/appropriateness arm means and their uncertainty appear only graphically, descriptive-richness SDs and numerical SEs are not printed, and Figure 7's numerical bootstrap intervals and p values are absent (PDF pp. 16, 20-23). The data are available only on request (PDF p. 27); authors' tables or data would settle these extraction gaps, which do not affect eligibility.

ALP card content: Section 4.4.2 names persona names and demographic sketches, while Appendix A requests additional motivations, frustrations, and scenario suggestions (PDF pp. 11, 30). The exact details displayed on the cards are not specified; authors' interface materials would settle exposure to the additional content, without changing eligibility.
notes: Not listed as outcomes, because they are not scored on the output or are not arm contrasts: self-reported mental demand, trust, user control, perceived AI role, and ownership (Table 2, Section 5.2); process measures (task duration, interaction count, artifact count, dialogue acts, transitions, entropy; Section 5.3, Table 3); within-condition correlations of entropy and AI-critique share with creativity and appropriateness (Section 5.3.2); vocabulary diversity, which appears only as a correlate of message length (PDF p. 24); Qwen3-32B ratings of the same rubric, used only as a validity check and not reported by condition. Baseline DAT scores (collected before the task, Figure 2) did not predict creativity (r_s = 0.026, p = .685; PDF p. 24). Figure 7 d values use the pooled SD, with 10,000-resample bootstrap CIs and Welch t-tests, Holm-corrected per outcome across six pairs; the CIs and p values are not printed. Contrasts use FD as the reference arm plus the paper's IC vs ALP contrast (and HLE vs IC for descriptive richness, where it survives Holm). The search-record lead ('without stated random assignment', 'no unit stated') is superseded: random assignment is stated on PDF p. 9, and N = 244 counts people. PDF page = journal page + 1 (publisher cover page). Final review: all markdown, including Appendices A-C, was read; challenged passages and retained outcome statistics were checked against PDF text and relevant figures. The unchanged reconciliation object is a historical record; the final object documents corrections that supersede its initial randomized-people count and descriptive-richness measure mapping. No reconciliation differences remain marked unresolved. The measure code for descriptive richness and the distinct-person randomized count are null where the available source does not support a value.

open_items.item: Primary ai_design contrast/reference choice: the documented FD prompt is rubric-guided, and no arm is a plain default; Atlas review can choose among the recorded contrasts without additional source material. No eligibility criterion depends on this choice.

Exact random element in sequential balancing: bears on criterion 1 if the procedure proves deterministic. The paper explicitly reports random assignment, so criterion 1 is currently met; authors' allocation protocol or code would settle the implementation.

Figure 2 versus Section 4.2 assignment/exclusion chronology: authors' participant-flow documentation would reconcile the source conflict. It does not alter the reported randomization or analyzed count used for eligibility.
Number of distinct people initially randomized: requires authors' deduplicated assignment flow and exclusion counts by reason. n_randomized is null; criterion 2 is met by 244 analyzed people.
Exclusions by arm and engagement-based attrition: authors could provide the flow by condition and exclusion reason. This affects bias assessment, while the three eligibility criteria remain met.
Preregistration registry, date, and scope: authors could supply the registration behind the quality-criteria claim. Preregistration is not required for eligibility.

Printed F/df/p inconsistencies and the HLE-versus-ALP richness effect-sign inconsistency: authors could supply corrected analysis output. Printed values remain recorded; no eligibility decision depends on significance or effect direction.

Descriptive-richness measure vocabulary: resolved by leaving measure null and retaining the source-defined elaboration measure. Any taxonomy expansion or pooling choice needs Atlas review, with no further source needed and no effect on criterion 3.

Direct arm-versus-arm diversity contrasts and numerical permutation-null means: authors could supply the underlying data and analysis output. The descriptive baseline is a different quantity; missing estimates do not affect eligibility.
Task taxonomy: creative_writing is supported by the narrative persona-and-scenario artifact; no further source is needed. Alternative labels would not change creative-task eligibility.

Unprinted arm means, uncertainty estimates, and Figure 7 bootstrap intervals/p values: authors could provide tables or participant data, which the paper says are available on request. These are extraction gaps, not eligibility gaps.

ALP card details actually displayed beyond names/demographic sketches: authors could supply interface materials. This clarifies exposure to generated scenario content without affecting the three criteria.
